original.a: Which of these is the product?

original.a: Which of these is the product?

original.ex: Newman–Kwart rearrangement: On strong heating an O-aryl thiocarbamate rearranges to the S-aryl thiocarbamate; hydrolysis then gives a thiophenol, so it turns phenols into thiophenols. Exchanging C=S for C=O drives it (about 13 kcal/mol). It is an intramolecular nucleophilic aromatic substitution, so electron-withdrawing ortho or para groups speed it up; palladium or photoredox catalysts let it run far cooler.
mc: The thiocarbonyl sulfur attacks the aryl carbon bonded to oxygen, through a four-membered cyclic transition state.
The aryl–O bond breaks as the aryl–S bond forms (an intramolecular nucleophilic aromatic substitution).
This gives the S-aryl thiocarbamate, with a strong C=O in place of the C=S.

original.a: Which of these is the product?

cond: Ir[dF(CF₃)ppy]₂(dtbbpy)PF₆, NiCl₂·glyme, dtbbpy, Cs₂CO₃, DMF, blue LEDs

original.ex: An amino acid loses CO₂ under photoredox catalysis and nickel couples the radical with an aryl halide. Two catalytic cycles: the excited iridium photocatalyst oxidises the carboxylate, which loses CO₂ to give a nucleophilic α-amino radical, and nickel joins that radical to the aryl group. Trifluoroborates, silicates and C–H bonds (via HAT) serve as radical sources too.
mc: Blue light excites the Ir(III) photocatalyst, which oxidises the caesium carboxylate by single-electron transfer.
The carboxyl radical loses CO₂, leaving a nucleophilic α-amino radical.
Meanwhile Ni(0) adds oxidatively into the aryl bromide, giving Ar–Ni(II)–Br.
The alkyl radical adds to nickel, giving Ar–Ni(III)(alkyl)Br.
Reductive elimination forms the C–C bond and leaves Ni(I)Br.
The reduced photocatalyst, Ir(II), turns Ni(I) back into Ni(0), closing both cycles (radical capture by Ni(0) before oxidative addition is also proposed).

original.a: Which of these is the product?
original.ex: Mild dehydrating agent: secondary and tertiary alcohols to alkenes by syn-elimination. Here only one alkene can form, since a bridgehead alkene is impossible. An alcohol with two kinds of β-hydrogen gives a mixture: 2-methylbutan-2-ol gives the more and the less substituted alkene 2.4 : 1. Primary alcohols give carbamates instead; primary amides give nitriles.
mc: The alcohol attacks sulfur and displaces triethylamine, giving a sulfamate ester.
On gentle heating the C–O bond starts to ionise, and the carbamate nitrogen abstracts a β-hydrogen on the same side (syn, Ei).
The alkene forms before the cation can rearrange; only C3 can lose its hydrogen, since a bridgehead alkene is impossible.

original.ex: Azo radical initiator: on heating to about 65–85 °C it loses N₂, giving 2-cyanoprop-2-yl radicals that start radical chains. A few mol% is enough, since it only starts the chain (by making Bu₃Sn•). Here the aryl radical cyclises 5-exo onto the allyl ether. Et₃B/O₂ starts chains at room temperature or below.
mc: AIBN loses N₂ on heating, giving 2-cyanoprop-2-yl radicals that abstract H from Bu₃SnH.
Bu₃Sn• abstracts bromine, giving the aryl radical.
The aryl radical cyclises 5-exo onto the allyl ether, giving a primary radical.
The primary radical abstracts H from Bu₃SnH, giving 3-methyl-2,3-dihydrobenzofuran and a new Bu₃Sn•.
